headline: Indian-American Astrophysicist Sukanya Chakrabarti Elected Fellow of American Physical Society
subheadline: The University of Alabama in Huntsville professor was honored for novel and sustained contributions to understanding dark matter, measured through the tiny accelerations it produces in stars and pulsars.
body:
• Dr. Sukanya Chakrabarti, Pei-Ling Chan Endowed Chair at The University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH), has been elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society (APS), one of the physics community's most selective honors.
  • The APS citation credits her novel and sustained contributions to understanding dark matter, based on extreme-precision dynamical measurements and pioneering work on binaries hosting compact objects.
  • Her method measures the tiny accelerations dark matter produces in pulsars, stars and eclipsing binaries to map dark-matter clumps in the Milky Way — a route toward answering what dark matter is.
  • APS Fellowship is tightly capped: recommended nominees each year may not exceed one-half of 1% of the Society's current non-student membership.

Dr. Sukanya Chakrabarti, an astrophysicist at The University of Alabama in Huntsville, has been elected a Fellow of the American Physical Society for her work on dark matter, UAH announced. Chakrabarti holds the Pei-Ling Chan Endowed Chair in the College of Science at UAH, which is part of The University of Alabama System.

She was selected by the American Physical Society's Division of Astrophysics and elected by the APS Council of Representatives. The university described the Fellowship as one of the physics community's most selective professional honors, recognizing exceptional contributions to the field.

What the citation says

The citation for Chakrabarti's Fellowship reads: "For novel and sustained contributions to the understanding of dark matter based on the development of extreme-precision dynamical measurements, as well as pioneering considerations of binaries hosting compact objects."

The selectivity is structural. According to UAH, the number of recommended nominees for APS Fellowship each year may not exceed one-half of 1% of the Society's current non-student membership, so election marks a body of work judged exceptional by peers rather than a single result.

"We have been developing new ways to map dark matter by measuring the extraordinarily small accelerations it produces in stars throughout our Galaxy."

— Dr. Sukanya Chakrabarti, University of Alabama in Huntsville

Mapping what cannot be seen

Dark matter is invisible material that makes up much of the universe, and Chakrabarti's research approaches it through gravity rather than light. She uses extremely precise measurements of pulsars and binary stars — pairs of stars orbiting each other — to detect the subtle gravitational pull of dark matter in the Milky Way, according to UAH.

By combining extreme-precision measurements of stars, pulsars and eclipsing binaries, her team aims to detect dark-matter clumps on increasingly small scales. Those clumps, she said, carry the fingerprints of dark-matter models and could help answer a fundamental question in physics: what dark matter is. The approach brings together theoretical astrophysics, observational astronomy, computational methods and precision measurements, and it is producing a kind of cosmic map that reveals invisible matter by watching how it makes stars move.

Chakrabarti said she was deeply honored by the recognition and grateful for the support at UAH, which lets her continue measurements that bring together time-domain astronomy and precision measurements.

Earlier work at UAH

Chakrabarti joined UAH in 2022. The same year, she led the discovery of the first stellar-mass black hole around a Sun-like star from the Gaia mission, according to the university. Her work has contributed to UAH's growing prominence in astrophysics and space science and provides opportunities for students and researchers there to take part in investigations of some of the most challenging questions in modern physics.

Why it matters for the diaspora

For the Indian-American scientific community, Chakrabarti's election is a concrete marker of diaspora researchers reaching the top tier of American physics on work that defines a field — in this case, a new way to measure a substance that has never been directly seen. Her base at a public university in Huntsville also puts that research in a teaching institution, where students work directly on the measurements behind the honor.

What happens next

The next step in the research program is scale: larger samples of precise stellar and pulsar measurements, aimed at detecting dark-matter clumps on smaller scales and distinguishing between competing dark-matter models. If those clumps can be mapped reliably, astronomers gain a test of theories that have so far rested largely on indirect evidence from galaxy behavior.
